If you go down afterwards, try the portal of the Palace of the Governors as a frame, with people and adobe walls in the foreground. text.description:
Canyon Road is a street of galleries in Santa Fe, and it is one of the easiest places in town to take a good phone photo. The low adobe-style buildings line both sides, the street runs east toward the foothills, and at the far end the hills fill the background. That gives you a ready-made picture with a clear foreground, middle and distance.

The best first frame is at the western end, where Canyon Road meets Paseo de Peralta. From there you look along the street towards the hills. The galleries lead the eye along the route and the hills rise ahead of you. Guides suggest starting here and walking east, because the mountains stay in front of you and the composition works better that way.

Once you have that opening shot, wander up the street and look for smaller scenes. At the corner with Delgado Street there is an old wooden gate set in an adobe wall. It makes a closer doorway-and-wall picture that contrasts nicely with the long view.

Stick to the public sidewalk for your photos, and ask before photographing artwork or courtyards inside galleries. Parking is limited, so it helps to arrive on foot. Take your time, because the street rewards slow walking and a few different angles.
text.geographic_location: Canyon Road runs east from Paseo de Peralta toward the foothills in Santa Fe. The photo spot is at its western end, where the two streets meet.
text.directions_text: There are no Santa Fe stations or tram stops at this spot, so walk or take a taxi to the corner of Canyon Road and Paseo de Peralta. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the opening view along the street, as it shows the galleries and hills in a natural way. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the sky and the road. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the hills or a gate and wall without walking up to them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Face along the street, which runs away from you to the south-east, with the galleries lining the route and the foothills at the far end. For the alternative view, walk to the corner of Delgado Street for the old wooden gate and adobe wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the road in the lower middle of the frame, with the hills along the upper third. Keep the walls on both sides fairly even so the street leads the eye. Wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or let one walker add scale. At Delgado Street, move in close and frame the gate against the wall, using the street behind it as a softer background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the adobe wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the walls are not washed out. Use portrait mode for the gate and wall if you want the background softened.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The last 90 minutes before sunset, when low light warms the adobe walls. Some guides suggest morning for the shadows, then a return in late afternoon to catch the other side of the road.

text.access_note: Canyon Road is a public street and you can photograph from the sidewalk, but ask before photographing artwork or courtyards inside galleries, and check the official site before you go for gallery details.

text.description:
San Miguel Chapel is a small adobe church, and it suits a phone camera well. The front is plain and earthy, with a single tower and a stone wall around it. That gives you clean shapes, soft textures and a lot of sky above the roofline. It sits right on Old Santa Fe Trail, which also went by its older name, College Street. That makes it a good place to shoot the building as part of a street scene rather than as an isolated monument.

The most useful viewpoint is the public sidewalk on Old Santa Fe Trail, looking across the street at the chapel. From here you get the chapel's front. The Pink Adobe restaurant at 406 Old Santa Fe Trail is directly across the street from the chapel, so it will be behind you at this spot. The restaurant is private, so stay on the sidewalk and keep out of its entrance.

The chapel is consecrated and holds sacraments during Mass, so don't photograph during services. If you want a different look, walk to the corner of Old Santa Fe Trail and De Vargas Street. From there you can catch the side and the front of the chapel at an angle, much as an old historic photograph of the building was taken. Keep other pedestrians and passing traffic in mind while you frame your shot, and take your time: the street is part of the picture, but you only need a minute or two to get the shot.

The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole chapel front and a bit of the street fit in. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you need to fit in more of the street, and keep the chapel away from the edges, where lines can stretch. A 2x telephoto setting, if your phone has it, is good for the tower and the stone wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From here the photo shows the chapel's front. Stay on the public sidewalk, not on the restaurant's property.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with one of the vertical lines so the walls stay upright. For a different angle, try the corner of Old Santa Fe Trail and De Vargas Street, which shows the side and front of the chapel together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the chapel wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the adobe does not wash out. If cars or people pass, a Live Photo lets you pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters adobe walls. Visit outside Mass times so you are not photographing during a service.

For practical advice, walk slowly along the approach and look for a sculpture that sits between you and the entrance. Let it fill one side of the frame and leave the building on the other. Keep your phone level so the walls stay straight. Only the outdoor grounds are free to walk around. The galleries inside are paid, and special exhibitions can have their own photography rules. Drone flying is generally not permitted on Museum Hill, so check before flying.

text.description: The New Mexico State Capitol is known locally as the Roundhouse, and the nickname is the whole story of the photo: the building is round, so the best picture is a head-on view of that curve. The facade is in the Territorial style, and each of the four entrance wings has a carved State Seal above the doorway. That seal is a good detail to frame, because it is distinctive and sits neatly in the middle of the picture. The Capitol grounds are planted with high-desert plants, sequoias and sculptures by Allan Houser, so you can also step back and include some greenery and sculpture around the building. Stand at the front of the building by one of the entrance wings, hold the phone level and let the curve of the wall sweep across the frame. Then move in closer for a second shot of the seal over the entrance. Take a few steps sideways between shots, because the curve changes the look of the facade a lot from one spot to the next. Check for people crossing the entrance and wait a moment if you want a clean frame. Shoot the wide view and the close detail so you have both a scene-setter and a keepsake.

The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

text.description: The Palace of the Governors is the long, low adobe building on the north side of Santa Fe Plaza, at Palace Avenue. Its most recognisable feature is the long wooden portal (a covered porch) running along the front. It photographs well because the plaza gives you open space to step back and take in the whole frontage, which is hard to do on most streets. The simplest shot is from the central obelisk, looking across the plaza to the north side. The obelisk sits in the foreground and the earthy adobe wall and wooden portal fill the background. It also works for a posed photo of friends or family, with the Palace behind them. Up close, the carved portal beams and the low facade make good detail shots. Native American artisans regularly set out their wares under the portal, which adds colour and life to a close-up. Stall positions and the number of vendors change from day to day, so you may need to wait a moment for people to move out of the frame. Guides describe the plaza as the city's most photographed public space and say it is calmest at first light, before the shops open. For a clear, uncluttered view of the building, go early. text.description: The Oldest House is a small adobe building at 215 East De Vargas Street, a short walk south-east of the plaza in Santa Fe. That claim is disputed, so treat the plaque as part of the story rather than settled fact. The street also helps the picture, because the San Miguel Chapel is close by and can sit in the same scene. This is one of the quieter, more human-scale shots on the map. It works best as a straightforward street-level photo, not a grand view. Stand on East De Vargas Street, facing the house's front wall, and take in the adobe front with the plaque and the street around it. Keep the whole front wall in view so the plaque and the doorway both read clearly, then take a closer second shot of the plaque for the caption. The house sits just east of Old Santa Fe Trail, so you can also use the street itself as a leading line. Wait a moment if a passer-by walks into the frame; a little life in the street adds scale to such a small building.

text.description:
The New Mexico Museum of Art stands on the northwest corner of the Plaza in the middle of Santa Fe, where Palace Avenue meets Lincoln Avenue. It is built in the Pueblo Revival style, with soft adobe-toned walls, wooden beams (vigas) and wooden balconies. Guides often call it one of Santa Fe's most photographed buildings, and the street corner gives you the standard postcard angle.

It photographs well because the two street sides meet at the corner and the edge of the Plaza gives you a natural frame. Stand at the corner and you get the Palace Avenue front and the Lincoln Avenue side in one shot, with the street leading the eye towards the building.

If you have time, there are two other angles. From West Palace Avenue you can face the main facade straight on and see the vigas and balconies clearly. Lincoln Avenue shows the quieter side of the building, with its own mission-style facade and the street in the foreground. Treat that one as an extra to try, not a certainty, as it is the least proven of the three.

The courtyard and sculpture garden inside are paid-entry, so this guide sticks to the street views. Keep your phone level so the walls and balcony lines stay straight, and leave a little space around the roofline so the building does not look cramped.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Santa Fe, on the northwest corner of the Plaza, where Palace Avenue meets Lincoln Avenue.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Plaza in central Santa Fe, then head for its northwest corner at Palace Avenue and Lincoln Avenue. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit both street sides in. Use 2x or the telephoto lens for details such as the vigas and wooden balconies.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Look north-west towards the Palace Avenue and Lincoln Avenue corner, where the Pueblo Revival front and both street sides meet, framed by the edge of the Plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the corner of the building with one of the vertical lines. Leave a little of the Plaza edge in the frame so the building has context. For a straight-on view of the adobe facade, walk to West Palace Avenue instead. For a quieter side view, try Lincoln Avenue and check the spot on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the adobe keeps its colour. Keep the phone upright to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on adobe walls. Go when the pavement is quieter if you want a clear view of the corner.

text.description:
The Santa Fe Railyard is a stretch of railway land in Santa Fe, where the historic Santa Fe Depot, the tracks and the restored water tower make a good mix of subjects for a phone. The best-known picture is the old depot building with trains on the tracks and the mountain range as a silhouette behind it. The depot is also where the Rail Runner arrives, so it makes an easy starting point for a photo walk around the Railyard.

There are several different pictures here, so you can take your time. Start at the depot, then continue to Railyard Plaza for the water tower standing over the paved plaza, with the Rail Runner tracks behind it and the Sangre de Cristo Mountains beyond. For something calmer, Casitas Picnic Grove West looks across the trees and paved paths toward the mountains, with the water tower to one side and a train in view.

One practical point: on Saturdays the Artisans and Farmers markets set up booths near the water tower, and these can block the view of it. The Santa Fe Artists Market runs on Saturdays from March to December. If the tower is your main picture, a non-market day may be easier. Conditions change, so check what is on before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Santa Fe, at the Railyard, around the Santa Fe Depot where the Rail Runner arrives. The depot sits at the edge of the Railyard.
text.directions_text: Arriving by Rail Runner, you reach the Santa Fe Depot at the edge of the Railyard. The water tower and Railyard Plaza are elsewhere in the Railyard. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the depot, the platforms and the trains. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the tracks and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the water tower or the mountain line behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. It is in front of the Santa Fe Depot on the track side, facing the platforms, so confirm on site that you are in that spot. From there the photo shows the historic depot building with trains on the tracks and the mountain range as a silhouette behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tracks up with a grid line so they lead the eye toward the depot and the mountains. Keep the horizon level. If you have time, a second view is from Railyard Plaza, which shows the water tower with the Rail Runner tracks and the Sangre de Cristo Mountains behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the depot or the train to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and mountains keep their colour instead of washing out. If a train is arriving, a Live Photo can help you pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try a non-market day so the water tower is clear. For the mountain silhouette, early or late in the day usually gives the most shape. Check which way the light falls when you arrive.

text.description:
The Cathedral Basilica of St. Francis of Assisi is a Romanesque-style church in downtown Santa Fe, built of warm, honey-coloured stone. Its twin towers, arched entrance and round rose window give it a calm, symmetrical face that suits a phone camera well. The classic picture is the whole facade seen head-on across the downtown plaza, and it looks best when late sun falls straight onto the stone and makes it glow.

The phone icon on the map is about 85 m west of the subject. From here you can take the facade head-on with both towers. The east end of Santa Fe Plaza is a separate viewpoint, from which both towers and the full front also fit into one frame. For a closer view, walk to Cathedral Place, in front of the church. There you can frame the arched doorway, the rose window and the towers with the bronze statue of St. Francis and the courtyard in the foreground. Cathedral Park is a third option: a shaded, grassy spot with benches where the church becomes the backdrop to a more relaxed, leafy shot.

Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. Take a few frames with different amounts of sky, and check the edges for passers-by. Photographing the interior is generally not allowed, especially during services, so plan on exterior pictures.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the doorway so the two towers balance left and right, and turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. For a different view, Cathedral Place gives close frontal shots of the arched entrance, rose window and towers with the bronze St. Francis statue in the foreground, and Cathedral Park gives a leafy, shaded setting with the church behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its colour. Use the 0.5x lens only when you are close, and keep the phone level to avoid leaning towers.

text.description: The red steel truss bridge is the picture most visitors come to the Santa Fe Botanical Garden for. It spans the Arroyo de los Pinos, and from the right spot the red frame stands out clearly against the piñon-juniper slopes and the distant mountains behind it. The bridge dates from the 1950s and was moved to the garden from a former highway site, which gives it a bit of local history as well as a strong shape. The red against the muted greens and browns of the high desert makes it an easy subject for a phone, because the colour does most of the work for you. Take your first shot with the bridge centred and the slopes filling the background. Then step a little to one side, so the bridge sits on a third of the frame and the hills and sky take the rest. If you want something softer afterwards, the Orchard Gardens section is a good alternative. There, fruit trees, wildflowers and grasses give you texture and seasonal colour rather than a single big subject. The native piñon-juniper woodland is also useful if you want to show the open high desert without formal beds. The Art Trail has uneven ground and one step, so watch your footing while you look at the screen. Check the garden's official site before you go for access details.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Step a few metres along the path to get the red steel truss bridge in frame over the arroyo, with the piñon-juniper slopes and distant mountains behind it. From the bridge itself you can instead photograph the arroyo and the slopes.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the bridge on one of the lines rather than dead centre, leaving the hills and mountains to fill the rest. Hold the phone steady and keep the horizon level. If you have time, take a second view in the Orchard Gardens, where the fruit trees, wildflowers and grasses make a softer, more textured picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red of the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little. This keeps the red rich and stops the bright sky from washing out the scene.

text.description:
Sena Plaza is a small, enclosed courtyard just off East Palace Avenue, and it feels quite different from the street outside. The ground is brick, and flowering fruit trees, benches and a fountain fill the space. Around the courtyard stands a two-level adobe building with covered porches. That mix of warm earthy walls, greenery and shaded walkways is why it works so well for phone photos. Everything is close together, so you can take wide views and small details from the same spot.

The best place to start is the brick patio near the fountain, inside the courtyard. From there you can see the trees, the benches and the two storeys of porches in one view. The courtyard can be busy with diners and shoppers, and the restaurant patio takes up much of the space, so you may need to shoot around the tables. Be polite about people's meals, and wait a moment if someone walks through your view. For a second picture, step back out to East Palace Avenue. From the pavement you can photograph the long street-facing adobe frontage with its portal, which makes a good scene-setting shot to go with the courtyard pictures. Afternoon is suggested for photographing the courtyard.

Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the fountain, a bench under the trees or the porch beams.

text.description:
Acequia Madre is the name of both a street and the old irrigation ditch that runs beside it, on Santa Fe's Historic Eastside. The photo here is a quiet, textured scene: a 1930s adobe house with carved gates and a courtyard wall, and the ditch running along in front of it. The earthy wall, the dark wood of the gates and the line of the ditch give you plenty of shapes to work with, and the whole thing reads clearly even on a small screen.

The corner is a well-known place to see the ditch and adobe architecture together, and the house is described as the most photographed home on the Historic Eastside. The house is private property, so take your pictures from the public sidewalk and do not step into the courtyard. Keep your voice down and be considerate of the neighbours, as this is a residential street.

Use what you see on the street as your guide. Include a little of the sidewalk or the ditch edge in the foreground so the picture has depth. Then move in for a tighter shot of the carved gate or the wall texture. If you want more of the ditch story, Monsignor Patrick Smith Park is where the ditch runs in the open behind the houses facing Canyon Road, and the ditch's first diversion gate is along the street. Water flow and access there may have changed, so treat those as a bonus rather than a promise.
text.geographic_location: Acequia Madre is on Santa Fe's Historic Eastside, where the old irrigation ditch runs alongside the street near the Garcia Street area. A further stretch of the ditch runs through Monsignor Patrick Smith Park, behind houses facing Canyon Road.
text.directions_text: Head for Acequia Madre near Garcia Street. The phone icon on the map is about 320 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the house, gates and ditch together. Switch to 2x or the telephoto lens if your phone has one, to pick out the carved gates and wall texture without leaving the sidewalk. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can help if the street is tight, but keep the gridlines on so the wall stays straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Start there, then walk east along the public sidewalk to the southeast corner by the house. Once at the corner you should see the 1930s adobe house with its carved gates and courtyard wall, with the ditch running in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to line the courtyard wall up with a horizontal line, and let the ditch run through the lower part of the frame as a leading line. Then take a second, closer shot of the carved gate. If you have time, the ditch's first diversion gate along the street or Monsignor Patrick Smith Park make a different take on the same subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the adobe keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. Stay on the sidewalk and don't enter the courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters adobe walls and carved wood, and the street tends to be calmer then.

text.access_note: The corner is a public sidewalk, but the house itself is private property, so photograph from the sidewalk only.

text.description: Cristo Rey Church is a large adobe church at the upper end of Canyon Road, on the street that carries its name. It is worth a short stop because the soft, earthy bulk of the building sits well against the hillside behind it. The best phone view is from the corner where Canyon Road meets Cristo Rey Street. From there the church is framed by the street and the slope around it, and you can fit the whole mass of the building into one photo. The upper end of Canyon Road is quieter than the gallery stretch lower down, which makes it easier to stand and compose without people crossing your frame. If you want the classic straight-on view, the church's full front façade with its garden in the foreground is the alternative. Plan on exterior shots only, as the building may be closed. Addresses can vary, so check on the day rather than relying on a street number. Take one wide shot of the corner, then a closer one of the walls and doorway. Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines so the walls don't lean.
text.geographic_location: Cristo Rey Church stands at the upper end of Canyon Road in Santa Fe, where Cristo Rey Street meets it. It is on the quieter side of the road, above the gallery section.
text.directions_text: Head for the upper end of Canyon Road in Santa Fe. From there the church is about 93 m to the west, a short walk of around a minute. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner view with the street and hillside around the church. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you need more of the building, and keep the phone level so the walls don't curve. Try telephoto (2x) for close shots of the walls and doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From here the photo shows the church's adobe bulk framed by the street and the surrounding hillside. For the alternative, the straight-on front façade with its garden, walk towards the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and line the church up so the walls stand straight. Let the street run along the lower part of the frame and keep the hillside as a backdrop. For the second viewpoint, the front façade with the garden in the foreground, place the garden low in the frame and the façade above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the adobe wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the wall keeps its colour and texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and warms the adobe. The upper end of Canyon Road is also likely to be quieter than the gallery section.
